audits.mathematicalReason: The net contains all six faces of the cube, so an edge length s satisfies 6s² = 18. Thus s² = 3 and, since an edge length is positive, s = √3 cm. The volume is s³ = 3√3 cm³. The surface-area and cube-volume scopes directly support this method, with the principal square root supplying the positive edge length.

figureEvidence.fact: The nonoverlapping net consists of six congruent squares: four in a row, one below the second square, and one above the fourth.

audits.mathematicalReason: Normalize the square's side length to 1. The given ratios give AF = CD = 2/3 and FE = DE = 1/3. The three corner triangles ABF, BCD, and EFD have areas 1/3, 1/3, and 1/18. Therefore [BFD]/[ABCE] = 1 − 1/3 − 1/3 − 1/18 = 5/18. This validates the triangle-area and composite-area subtraction method. Alternatively, E=(0,0), B=(1,1), F=(0,1/3), and D=(1/3,0) give the same result by shoelace. The coordinate route is a valid alternative, not an additional required method.

figureEvidence.fact: F lies on side AE and D lies on side EC of square ABCE.
Segments BF, BD, and FD partition the square into triangle BFD and the three corner triangles ABF, BCD, and EFD.

audits.mathematicalReason: The outer and inner radii are 2 inches and 1 inch, so the tape's annular cross-sectional area is π(2² − 1²) = 3π in². In the usual tightly packed, unstretched-tape model, unrolling produces a rectangular cross section of length L and thickness 0.015 inches. Thus 0.015L = 3π, giving L = 200π ≈ 628.3 inches, which rounds to 600 inches to the nearest 100. Subtracting the disk areas fits cnm_p150's general description of adding or subtracting known areas; the circle and rectangle formulas, decimal division, and rounding provide the supporting calculations.

figureEvidence.fact: The shaded tape occupies the annulus between concentric circular boundaries.
The outer diameter is labeled 4 inches and the inner diameter is labeled 2 inches; these are diameters, not radii.

audits.mathematicalReason: The counterclockwise movement exceeds the clockwise movement by 3¾ − 2¼ = 1½ revolutions. Discarding the complete revolution leaves a half-turn counterclockwise. A half-turn takes west to east. Directional rotation is the assessed concept, and fractional subtraction supports this calculation.

figureEvidence.fact: The compass labels north at the top, east at the right, south at the bottom, and west at the left.
The spinner's initial arrow points left toward west.

audits.mathematicalReason: Complete the polygon to an 8 by 9 rectangle. The rectangular notch has height DE = BC − FA = 9 − 5 = 4. Its area is 8·9 − 52 = 20, so its width EF is 20/4 = 5. Consequently DE + EF = 4 + 5 = 9. Composite-area subtraction is the central procedure, supported by rectangle properties and the rectangle-area formula.

figureEvidence.fact: Right-angle markings at A, B, C, D, and F establish the rectilinear L-shaped boundary, with E as its inward corner.
AB is labeled 8, BC is labeled 9, and FA is labeled 5. The missing lower-left rectangle has width EF and height DE.

audits.mathematicalReason: Use unit coordinates with the grid's upper-left corner at (0,0). The upper-left blade has boundary vertices (2.5,2.5), (0,1), (1,1), and (1,0). Joining the center to the inward corner (1,1) splits this blade into two triangles. Each has base 1 and perpendicular height 2.5 − 1 = 1.5, hence area 3/4. Each blade therefore has area 3/2, and the four blades have total area 4·(3/2) = 6. This directly supports composite-area decomposition with triangle area as the supporting procedure.

figureEvidence.fact: The figure is a five-by-five grid of equal unit squares, and the four shaded blades meet at the grid's center.
The upper-left blade has outer tips at (0,1) and (1,0), with its inward right-angled corner at (1,1); the other blades repeat this configuration by quarter-turns.

audits.mathematicalReason: The cylinder has radius 8/2 = 4 cm and axial length 6 cm, so its volume is π·4²·6 = 96π cm³. The depicted planar cut runs between opposite rim points at opposite ends and passes through the cylinder's center. A half-turn about a suitable transverse diameter swaps the two resulting pieces, so the wedge has half the cylinder's volume: 48π ≈ 150.8 cm³. The closest choice is 151. The one-half factor is justified by this particular centered cut, not by an arbitrary wedge.

figureEvidence.fact: The cylinder's axial length is labeled 6 cm and its circular-end diameter is labeled 8 cm.
The oblique cut meets the bottom rim of the left end and the top rim of the right end, giving the centered slant cut used in the equal-volume argument.

audits.mathematicalReason: External tangency gives distance 2r between adjacent outer centers and distance r+1 from the central center to every outer center. The outer-center quadrilateral has four equal sides and is cyclic about the central center, so it is a square of side 2r. Its center-to-vertex distance is √(r²+r²) = r√2. Thus r+1 = r√2 and r = 1/(√2−1) = 1+√2, which is positive. Alternatively, a 45-degree right triangle gives sin 45° = r/(r+1), producing the same equation. Both proposed routes and their associated support scopes are defensible.

figureEvidence.fact: Each of the four congruent outer circles is externally tangent to its two adjacent outer circles.
The central radius-1 circle is externally tangent to all four radius-r circles, establishing equal central-to-outer center distances.
